items.prompt: An agent in org-A requests GET /api/tickets/ticket-B-999, a real ticket owned by org-B. What response do they get, and why that code?
items.answer: 404: findById filters by id AND the caller's organizationId, so the row is invisible
distractors: 403 Forbidden: the tenant middleware compares the ticket's organization with the caller's
200 with the ticket, because agents may read every ticket in the database regardless of organization
401 Unauthorized: the JWT was minted for another organization and is rejected
items.explanation: Tenant isolation lives in the query: where { id, organizationId }. A null result becomes AppError('Ticket not found', 404), which leaks nothing about other tenants.

items.answer: That an organizationId in the params or body matches the user's, letting requests without one pass
distractors: That every resource id in the URL belongs to the caller's organization, by looking each one up in the database
That the JWT's organization claim matches the subdomain in the Host header of the request
That the caller's role is allowed to act on the organization named in the query string
items.explanation: The middleware compares req.params.organizationId and req.body.organizationId with the user's org and 403s on mismatch; ticket ids are protected by the repository's organizationId filter, not here.

items.prompt: A user is deactivated (isActive false) while holding a still-valid access token. What does authenticate do on their next request?
items.answer: Rejects it with 401, as the user is reloaded on each request and isActive is checked
distractors: Lets it through until the 15-minute token expires, because the JWT payload is trusted
Returns 403 Forbidden with a 'deactivated' message so the client can show a specific error
Refreshes the token automatically and logs the user out on the client side
items.explanation: authenticate verifies the token, then prisma.user.findUnique(...) and throws if !user || !user.isActive; the catch converts every failure into AppError('Unauthorized', 401).

items.prompt: A requester tries to move their own OPEN ticket straight to RESOLVED. What happens?
items.answer: 400 Invalid transition: the state machine only lets OPEN move to IN_PROGRESS
distractors: 403 Forbidden: requesters can never change the status of a ticket
200 OK: requesters may resolve their own tickets from any state
200 OK, but the ticket is moved to IN_PROGRESS instead of RESOLVED
items.explanation: changeStatus first restricts requesters to RESOLVED or CLOSED targets, then calls canTransition(ticket.status, status); ALLOWED_TRANSITIONS[OPEN] is [IN_PROGRESS].

items.prompt: During changeStatus the database connection drops right after the ticket row is updated. What is the resulting state?
items.answer: The ticket shows the new status, but there is no STATUS_CHANGED activity or audit event
distractors: Nothing changed: Prisma rolls back the ticket update once any later write fails
The activity row exists but the status is unchanged, as the activity is written first
The audit event is written first, so the change is at least audited in every case
items.explanation: The update, the activity create and auditService.logEvent are three separate awaits on the base client; the guide's fix is to run all three through tx inside prisma.$transaction.

items.prompt: The drill asks whether assignTicket's logs can end up out of sync. What is the correct answer?
items.answer: Yes: the update, the ASSIGNED activity and the audit event are all separate writes
distractors: No: assignTicket validates the assignee first, so nothing can fail after the update
No: the repository update runs in a transaction that includes the audit service
Only if the assignee is a REQUESTER: that case writes logs before the update
items.explanation: Validation happens before the writes, but the three writes themselves are unconnected awaits; validation does not make them atomic.

items.prompt: The comments endpoint hides internal notes from requesters. A requester instead calls GET /api/tickets/:id on their own ticket. Are internal notes hidden there too?
items.answer: No: findById includes every comment with no isInternal filter, so internal notes reach the requester
distractors: Yes: getTicket strips isInternal comments for requesters before returning, mirroring the comments service
Yes: Prisma applies the comments service's where clause to every include of the comments relation
The request fails with 403, because requesters may only read comments through the comments endpoint
items.explanation: Only CommentsService.getComments adds where.isInternal = false for requesters; the ticket repository's include: { comments } has no such filter, the pitfall the guide lists as 'allowing requesters to read internal notes'.

items.prompt: ticketsRepository.update takes an organizationId parameter. What keeps a cross-tenant update from succeeding today?
items.answer: Only the earlier getTicket(id, organizationId, user), as the update's where is { id }
distractors: The update's where clause includes organizationId, so Prisma refuses any mismatched row
A compound unique index on (id, organizationId) declared in the Prisma schema
enforceTenantIsolation, which looks up the ticket's org before every PATCH
items.explanation: The repository's where is { id } alone (the comments in it debate the fix), which is exactly the 'querying by ID alone' pitfall; safety depends on every caller remembering the prior scoped read.

items.prompt: The ticket list's queryKey is ['tickets', page, status, priority, search, sortBy, sortDirection]. If a developer dropped status from the key, what would break?
items.answer: Changing the status filter would keep showing the cached page for the previous filter
distractors: Nothing: queryFn reads status from the URL, so the query refetches when it changes
The list would refetch on every render, because keys without filters are never cached
TypeScript would refuse to compile, as queryFn uses a variable missing from the key
items.explanation: The query key works like a dependency array: TanStack Query only fetches a new entry when the key changes. Leaving a parameter out is the first pitfall in the guide.

items.prompt: After a successful status change on the detail page, which cached queries are invalidated?
items.answer: Only ['ticket', id], so the list entries keyed ['tickets', ...] stay stale after it
distractors: Every query starting with 'ticket', which also prefix-matches the ['tickets', ...] list entries
['ticket', id] and ['comments', id], the same pair as the comment mutation
None: the page patches the cached ticket object in place without a refetch
items.explanation: handleStatusChange calls invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['ticket', id] }) only. Prefix matching is per array element, so 'ticket' does not match 'tickets'.

items.prompt: Why does the comment mutation invalidate ['comments', id] and ['ticket', id] instead of pushing the new comment into the cached array?
items.answer: A refetch returns server truth, including generated columns and other actors' changes
distractors: TanStack Query caches are read-only and cannot be changed with setQueryData after a fetch
Invalidation is synchronous, while patching the array would need an extra network round trip
The POST response is empty, so there is nothing to insert into the cached array
items.explanation: The guide's senior aside: real systems have multiple concurrent actors, so fetching from the server gets the exact truth including auto-generated database columns.

items.prompt: Which systems-level gap does the critique report about ticket path parameters?
items.answer: Ticket UUIDs in the path reach Postgres without Zod checks, so bad strings hit the DB
distractors: Path parameters are validated twice, by Zod and by Prisma, which slows every request
Path parameters are trusted for the organization id instead of the JWT claim
Path parameters are URL-decoded twice, enabling double-encoding attacks
items.explanation: The controller passes req.params.id straight into ticketsService.getTicket; the critique names 'no path param validation' as gap 3.

items.front: Rule for tenant isolation in repository queries?
items.back: Never look a record up by id alone. Pass the tenant id from the verified user (never the request body) down to the query, e.g. where { id, organizationId }, so a foreign row returns null and becomes a 404.

items.front: Ticket findById includes all comments, and getTicket returns it to requesters unfiltered. Risk and fix?
items.back: Requesters see internal notes on GET /tickets/:id even though the comments endpoint hides them. Filter the include by isInternal for requesters (or drop comments from the detail payload) and add a role-based test.

items.front: Ticket update, activity row and audit event are three separate awaits. Risk and fix?
items.back: A failure between writes leaves a status change with no activity or audit record. Wrap all three in prisma.$transaction(async (tx) => ...) using tx for every write, so any throw rolls back the batch.

items.front: What must go into a TanStack Query queryKey?
items.back: Every variable the queryFn depends on (page, filters, search, sort). The key is the cache identity: a changed key triggers a fetch, and a missing variable shows stale data for the old parameters.
